title: Russia’s Widening War on Europe
author: @foreignaffairs
text: Podcast Russia’s Widening War on EuropeA Conversation With Julianne Smith Published on October 8, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 60 minutes 00:00 / 1:00:16 0.5×1×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share Russia’s Widening War on Europe A Conversation With Julianne Smith Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/russias-widening-war-europehttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/russias-widening-war-europe Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details Since the start of the war in Ukraine almost five years ago, Russia has mounted ever more aggressive attacks in Europe, far from the battlefield. These attacks were long talked about as a form of “hybrid warfare.” But as Julianne Smith, the former U.S. ambassador to NATO, notes in a new piece in Foreign Affairs, they have reached a level of risk and flagrancy where that label may no longer apply. And these attacks come in the context of escalation in Ukraine and dissension in the transatlantic alliance, as the Trump administration calls into question basic commitments to Europe.Smith has warned of the dangers of Russian escalation and urged NATO to do more in response. Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke to her on Tuesday, October 6, about the options for raising the cost on Russia—as well as about the future of the war in Ukraine and the prospects for the United States and Europe in the wake of President Donald Trump.Sources:“Russia’s Hybrid War Has Entered a Dangerous New Phase” by Julianne Smith“The New Eurasian Order” by Julianne Smith and Lindsey Ford“NATO’s New Momentum: A Conversation With U.S. Ambassador to NATO Julianne Smith” The Foreign Affairs Interview“The Old World and the Middle Kingdom” by Julianne Smith and Torrey Taussig“Is a Post-American World Inevitable? A Conversation With Kurt Campbell, Rush Doshi, and Mark Leonard” The Foreign Affairs Interview“How Alliances Survive” by Kurt M. Campbell and Rush Doshi“The Abandoned Order” by Mark LeonardThis episode of The Foreign Affairs Interview was produced by Adelaide Parker and Kanishk Tharoor, with audio engineering by Todd Yeager and original music by Robin Hilton. Special thanks as well to Irina Hogan.This is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANJulie, thanks so much for being here. You were one of our very early guests on the podcast when you were U.S. ambassador to NATO, so it’s great to have you back.JULIANNE SMITHGreat to be back.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI want to start with the topic of your most recent piece for Foreign Affairs, just published. We’ve been hearing about the Russian hybrid campaign in Europe, especially since the start of the war in Ukraine almost five years ago. But in a sort of frog-boiling sense, I think people are only now stepping back and realizing just how much it’s escalated. If you could go back and tell yourself when you were U.S. ambassador to NATO five years ago exactly what we’d be seeing at this point, would you believe it? Would you be surprised? How do you understand this arc?JULIANNE SMITHI think if I were to go back and tell myself five years ago that this is where we would be today, with so much escalation in the Russian hybrid space, I think I would find it to be very hard to believe, and I’d be shocked by the ways in which Russia has escalated. I mean, we’ve seen two trends in recent years. I mean, first of all, to take a step back, Russian hybrid active measures, as they used to call them, they go back to the beginning of time. I mean, we’ve seen Russia use these types of efforts, relying on proxies to achieve political aims, these types of attacks, for many, many decades.What’s changed are two things. One, we’ve seen a significant uptick in the number of Russian hybrid attacks on NATO territory over the last couple of years. And by significant, I’m talking tripling and quadrupling, in some cases, the number of incidents. Number two, what Russia is doing is it’s shifting from plausible deniability. A key part of these attacks has always been Russia’s ability to deny what was happening, that it was not involved in these hybrid incidents, and they were keen to blame it on someone else, a rogue actor or the Ukrainians, their favorite villain.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd just to make this concrete, that might mean paying a down-on-his-or-her-luck Ukrainian or European to set a fire in a factory or something like that.JULIANNE SMITHRight. They essentially tap into organized criminal networks, and they ask people to do nefarious things. And they may hand them a bag of cash and ask them to go burn down a factory that produces drones or a weapons depot. And then the person slips away into the night, often not even understanding who is actually handing them the bag of cash and for what purposes. And so those proxies have always been kind of a key component.But Russia now is drifting into a new era where they don’t seem particularly concerned about plausible deniability. Russia is undertaking acts or attacks that are, in essence, undeniable. And the best example of that would be the recent incident in Germany, where three explosive-laden drones were found near or on Leipzig Airport. One hit a Ukrainian cargo plane, one touched a commercial jet, and one was found a little distance away from the airport itself. But this was an incident where Russia hardly tried to make an effort to conceal what it was doing. And so these two things together, the uptick in hybrid attacks in Europe paired with this new era where they don’t seem interested in even denying that they’re doing it, should be cause for concern for the NATO alliance. And that’s kind of where we find ourselves today.DAN KURTZ-PHELANWhat distinguishes that drone attack on the Leipzig Airport from a straightforward act of war? It seems like it would stretch the definition of hybrid to use that term here.JULIANNE SMITHWell, it’s interesting. We’re entering a period right now where essentially it’s hard to put the hybrid label on what Russia is doing. I mean, it used to be that these hybrid attacks never really touched kinetic action. So they took the form of disinformation campaigns, cyberattacks, occasionally an airspace violation. But now what we’ve seen in Leipzig and certainly in many other corners of Europe are incidents that are essentially bordering on all-out kinetic attacks. And so some folks in Europe running around NATO headquarters or in national capitals are asking themselves, “Are we even describing this in the right way? Is this not a movement towards kinetic action that’s drifting towards conventional warfare that could trigger an Article 5 response on behalf of the alliance?”DAN KURTZ-PHELANWhat is your understanding of Russian objectives here and what explains the Russian escalation? Is there a theory to this, or a strategy, or is it a reaction to setbacks in Ukraine or struggles in Ukraine? What’s your best guess?JULIANNE SMITHWell, Russia has had two standard objectives with hybrid warfare. Pretty simple: one, they always like to try to break down the unity and resolve that exists across the alliance. And two, they always want allies to doubt NATO’s Article 5 commitment, and whether or not it will hold in a crisis. And so by testing the alliance, they create some anxiety about whether or not the alliance, and particularly the United States right now, will show up if this starts to take a turn for the worse. So those are the two classic reasons that Russia has opted often to rely on hybrid attacks.The new rationale behind hybrid attacks is tied directly to Europe’s support for Ukraine. In light of the fact that the United States has taken its foot off the gas in Ukraine, no longer providing any form of security assistance, we now have a situation where Europe has really stepped up. Not every member of the NATO alliance, but most of the members of the NATO alliance and across the European Union are now trying to fill that gap and provide security assistance to Ukraine. And Russia wants to ensure that those states, those countries understand that that support comes at a cost. And so he’s doing his very best to prove to them in real time that the more you support Ukraine, the more you’re going to experience these types of hybrid attacks.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYour piece makes very clear that Europe and the NATO alliance more broadly have struggled to figure out the right response to these attacks, and it has certainly not deterred them, as we can see from this escalation. If you go back to the debates following the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, what were the discussions about the right strategy that NATO should take in response? And why has it been so hard? Why has Europe struggled so much to come up with a deterrence formula?JULIANNE SMITHWell, it is extraordinarily difficult for the alliance to grapple with Russian hybrid warfare. It is not a case where Russia is rolling tanks across NATO territory. And in that case, NATO’s 77 years of experience would trigger a very clear response. NATO knows what to do when it comes under a conventional attack. Where things get complicated is when he relies on these types of hybrid attacks: cutting an undersea cable, turning the lights out on a city in Europe for a couple of hours, flying into NATO airspace either with drones or MiGs or one asset or another. And there I think the alliance struggles to come to some collective decision on what costs it should impose on Moscow and what kind of a response it should have.I don’t want to give you the impression that NATO’s been sitting on its hands. When I was there at NATO, we talked a lot about sharpening our response options. We talked about the need to move quicker on attribution. Call out the Russians as soon as you know it, make sure they know and the world knows that they’re responsible for it. We were doing a better job at getting country systems back online when they came under some sort of cyberattack. And we put all sorts of new monitoring programs in place in the Baltic Sea, particularly to monitor what was happening with undersea cables.So it’s not fair to say that NATO has been asleep at the wheel. I think what is fair to say is that the alliance has done an okay job with responding to these incidents, but hasn’t adequately come up with a plan to deter them and to ensure that Russia pays a price. And there, NATO really is relatively empty-handed. Now, it’s complicated because NATO doesn’t have the authority to expel Russian diplomats or impose sanctions. That’s not in NATO’s lane; it’s a military alliance. But there are things that individual allies could do, or, working through the NATO alliance, they could sharpen the ways in which they signal to Russia that they will deter against these attacks and that Russia will pay a price at the end of the day.DAN KURTZ-PHELANWhat’s the right way of escalating the response from European governments and U.S. supporters, to the extent Washington is interested in that at this point, to respond adequately to what you’re describing as a fundamentally new phase in Russia’s offensive here?JULIANNE SMITHWell, first of all, I want to note that for our seven-plus decades across the alliance, the United States has played a critical leadership role in pushing the alliance towards response options and enhancing deterrence writ large against a whole variety of threats. And right now we do have a situation where the United States, in my mind, isn’t exactly leading in this space. The priority for the current U.S. administration has been to get allies to spend more on their own defense. I support that objective, by the way, and applaud what the administration has been able to do in moving Europeans to spend more on their own defense.But by focusing so hard on that objective and priority, my assessment is that they’ve let go of some of the added responsibilities that the United States has to lead on this question of Russian hybrid warfare. And in fact, the president, when he has been asked repeatedly about these incidents, he has mixed reactions. Sometimes he says NATO should shoot these drones down. He seems like he’s leaning into the threat. Other times he brushes it off very quickly, claims it was a mistake, says Putin has no intention of starting a conflict with NATO. And so allies can’t quite understand how to read the United States right now, and they’ve noted that Secretary Hegseth recently shut down the planning at Cyber Command to move forward with offensive cyber operations against Russia. That seems to be a pretty clear indication that we’re going to open up the trade space here, and Russia certainly is reading it as a green light to do more and to escalate.So number one is: why isn’t the U.S. leading on this? And if the U.S. isn’t able or willing to lead on this particular issue, what other country in the alliance can step forward? And I know the UK and Estonia and Poland and a couple of others have tried to push this agenda forward, but honestly, without the United States, it’s hard to bring the collective weight of the alliance together to really impose real costs on Moscow for these incidents. And if we don’t do that, if we don’t find a way for NATO to shift gears here and move from essentially responding to these incidents to cost in position, then Putin is going to continue to escalate. And that’s where I think we really need to see greater work by the alliance to look at these attacks, not just incident by incident, on a case-by-case basis, but really look at them in the aggregate and start looking at patterns of activity that should trigger a bigger, larger-scale collective response on the part of the alliance.DAN KURTZ-PHELANWhat would it mean to impose costs meaningfully on Putin? He seems so willing to disregard so many things that other leaders would consider meaningful costs. Is there anything that you think would affect his decision-making here?JULIANNE SMITHWell, it’s hard to make that list. I mean, obviously, since the war in Ukraine started, we’ve tried on a number of fronts to impose sanctions. Again, this isn’t in NATO’s wheelhouse, but we’ve expelled diplomats, intel officers. I think where I could imagine adding to that list is looking at the shadow fleet that Russia runs through the Baltic Sea to evade sanctions. We’ve seen some individual countries, France in particular, really increasing the number of ships that it’s boarding, that it’s checking, to send a signal to Moscow that this behavior is being monitored and will not be tolerated. I think there’s more that the alliance could do in that regard. I think we could also give the supreme allied commander Europe, SACEUR, more pre-designated authorities to respond in the moment. He has been given some new authorities vis-à-vis Baltic air policing to improve the alliance’s ability to respond in real time, but I think we could do more in the maritime space, so that’s an area where there’s more work to be done.And then we’ve seen some interesting choices by individual NATO members. I would note that Norway recently seized a Russian vessel in Svalbard in the Arctic because of the fact that Russia was refusing to pay damages for a Ukrainian energy company that it had seized in Crimea. That’s a pretty creative solution on the part of the Norwegians. They felt like they had the legal basis to do that. But these are the types of things that NATO collectively should be looking at, and individual members could do more as well. We’ve seen the Baltic states and, again, the Norwegians and the Poles lean in, but where’s the rest of the alliance on this?Lastly, I would say direct messaging can have an impact. You’ll remember in the fall of 2022, Russia was guilty of some pretty intense nuclear saber-rattling, warning that it was going to rely on tactical nuclear weapons in Ukraine. Thankfully, that never came to pass, but there was a moment when there was a considerable amount of direct messaging coming from the White House directly to the Kremlin on this matter to help Russia understand that it would face, in the words of the national security advisor at the time, “catastrophic consequences” if it did opt to use tactical nuclear weapons, which again has not happened.So the question here is what kind of direct messaging can we pursue at the moment? How can the U.S. or other countries in the alliance lead? How can we arm SACEUR with better pre-designated authorities to act? How can we push countries to think creatively, as the Norwegians and the French are, in going after that Russian shadow fleet and that vessel up in Svalbard? So there are things on the list. Will any of those ultimately change Putin’s calculus? We can’t know for sure. But I think where we can conclude today is that right now his signal from the alliance is that he can keep going, and escalation is the way to go. And my concern is that at some point this crosses the line and leads to catastrophic loss of life, and then NATO is in a crisis because it will be potentially facing an Article 5 scenario.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd then you imagine that escalating to what could be all-out war. That’s the concern here.JULIANNE SMITHPotentially. And it raises this question about the degree to which the United States will come to the aid of the country that’s been attacked. The biggest fear in Europe right now is that the United States will not take any sort of Article 5 incident seriously and will fail to show up and support allies. And, of course, that would provide Putin with the perfect moment because then he would be able to show the world that NATO’s Article 5 commitment is really not worth the paper that it’s written on.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd that would be a more or less fatal blow to NATO.JULIANNE SMITHIndeed. Indeed.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI can imagine that if you’re in the German government or Baltic government or Polish government or any other European government, you’d want to do anything you can to invoke Article 5 for the next two years in that case.JULIANNE SMITHThat’s right. I think allies are concerned. And one really interesting data point on that is when the Germans found the three drones around or on Leipzig Airport, and they publicly announced that this was tied to the Russian state, they chose not to invoke Article 4 of the treaty, which is a special clause that allows countries to come in for an emergency session in the North Atlantic Council if they’re feeling like their security is under threat. And I thought it was interesting how Germany didn’t even want to go with Article 4. The message essentially from Berlin is, “We’ve got this. We don’t need to kind of start our engines in the NATO alliance.” And I wonder how other countries are reacting to that decision.We have seen cases where Poland and Estonia, they have asked for emergency Article 4 consultations, which have led the alliance to take some important steps in increasing its response options. But to me, that was very curious that Berlin came out definitively, pointed at Moscow, and yet chose not to ask for any special session at NATO headquarters.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDoes that decision, understandable as it is from Berlin’s perspective, itself erode NATO in the sense that Russia can see that allies are so resistant to actually using the alliance that it starts to lose its deterrent force?JULIANNE SMITHMy suspicion is that Moscow noted that with great interest, and is trying to see when allies do go for those Article 4 consultations and when they don’t, and what types of attacks trigger what kind of response either by a national government or by the NATO alliance. So, I mean, I don’t know if Russia is, it’s hard to say, reaching any definitive conclusions there, but my guess is they found that interesting, an interesting choice.It is also interesting because the German government has come out, one official claimed that Germany is now experiencing hybrid attacks on a daily basis. And so you’ve got this kind of alarmist position by this German official that this is something that we’re now witnessing each and every day in our country, and yet some hesitation there to bring that deeper into the alliance. No doubt the Germans briefed NATO allies in some session on what happened with the drones. But again, the Article 5 element of it is important, and could be sending Moscow the wrong signal.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou noted earlier that the context for this, or one of the drivers for this, is the fairly surprising, to me at least, increase in European support for Ukraine since the beginning of the Trump administration, the second Trump administration, and the decline in American support. Are you surprised by how much the Europeans have been willing and able to do to backfill for the reduction in U.S. support?JULIANNE SMITHI’m not that surprised. I think Europe didn’t get the credit that it deserved for the support that it put forward in the first few weeks and months of the war in Ukraine. Very quickly in 2022, we saw virtually every member of the alliance step forward and offer humanitarian, security, and economic assistance, and that ballooned out over time. I guess I wasn’t entirely sure whether or not they would be able to cover down on all forms of security assistance that the U.S. is providing. Certainly they’re not in a position to provide Patriots or other sophisticated air defense systems, but they’re doing their best to find alternatives.I mean, the real challenge for Europeans right now is that their stocks have thinned out considerably because of the generous support that they’ve been able to provide for almost five years now. And so my concern is: where do we go from here? I mean, there was a period last year where Europeans were purchasing kit from the United States to send to Ukraine. And now, given our depleted stocks in light of what we’re doing in Iran, I’m not sure there’s so much more that the Europeans can buy from us for Ukraine. So this will be an interesting challenge over the next year or two.Financially, Ukraine also is going to need a lot more support. So far, the Europeans have brushed off the idea of seizing the Russian assets that they froze at the start of the war. This is a highly controversial topic across Europe, fierce debates. I think they’re going to come back to that. And my hope is that they’re able to move the needle and free up those resources, without which I think it will be hard for them to maintain the very generous support for Ukraine that they’ve put forward over the last couple of years.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDo you worry about Ukraine this coming winter, given what looks like it’ll be major Russian escalation on civilian targets, especially in an attempt to break the political will of Ukraine? Where’s your level of anxiety about the Ukrainian ability to withstand that?JULIANNE SMITHI am very worried about the coming winter, and what appears to be a new phase where there’s just no red lines for Russia. I mean, they have not gone after all of Ukraine’s critical infrastructure over the last couple of years. They have frequently targeted civilians, let’s be clear, but the way in which they’re doing it now does seem to me to be an entirely new chapter. We’re seeing bridges targeted, more residential buildings coming in closer to Kyiv. They have not really targeted downtown Kyiv repeatedly over the years, and there seems to be a shift now in the approach. And so I am worried. I mean, look, the Ukrainians have surprised all of us with their incredible resilience and their resolve, and what they’ve been able to withstand frequently plunged into darkness and the cold and winter months. But the question is how much longer can the Ukrainian population withstand these types of attacks?I think the shortage of air defense systems now are really coming into play, and I’m just not sure where they’re going to turn. Again, Europe has, in some cases, countries have given almost all their own air defense away, exposing themselves. And so if they can’t get that from the United States and can’t find it in Europe, is it other countries around the world, the South Koreans? I mean, how creative can they get in finding the equipment that they need? So yes, this winter I think will be one to watch. And I am worried also because of the mixed signals that the U.S. is sending to Moscow, sometimes deeply concerned about the way in which Russia’s conducting the war and then oftentimes it feels like they’re looking away.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou can understand the, I think, Russian theory of success at this point, the combination of eroding European support and American support for Ukraine, and then trying to break the solidarity and will to resist among the Ukrainian people. If you’re thinking from the Ukrainian perspective, what is the right response? And if we’re trying to be optimistic, what’s a kind of plausible theory of success for Ukrainians over the next year or so?JULIANNE SMITHWell, Ukrainians are determined to fight on. And so Zelensky is traveling all over the world doing everything he can to remind people that Putin has turned up the volume and turned up the heat, that he’s increasingly targeting civilians, and that Zelensky urgently needs more air defense systems, most importantly. They’re very good at creating obviously autonomous systems like drones. They use them in such a sophisticated way. Someday we will all learn from this experience. But outside of those autonomous systems, they really do need air defense systems. So his goal is continue to maintain the world’s focus on his plight. Think more creatively about new partnerships. He’s moved to establish new relationships in the Middle East, which has been quite interesting and clever, I would say, on his part. Propping up his population, convincing them to keep calm and carry on. Ensuring that he can keep the lights on and the heat as best to his ability. And then pushing back on Russian aggression on the front.And they’ve had some victories, most often in single digits, a few kilometers here, a few kilometers there. But they have been getting much more creative and innovative with the ways in which they go after Russian supply lines, the Russian energy sector strikes deep into Russia and strikes in Moscow to help folks understand there that there is a war waging in Ukraine 24/7. So he’ll continue to do his very best, but I think we also have to understand what he’s up against. The politics get harder year by year for Zelensky. Mobilization challenges do get harder over time. And the economy, the economic state of Ukraine gets more and more difficult, I think, each month that this ticks by.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd it seems very hard to imagine what exactly would change Putin’s mind, would change his calculus at this point.JULIANNE SMITHYeah. I mean, you’ll remember there was a moment in the fall of ’25, when President Trump actually publicly talked about sending Tomahawks to Ukraine. I thought that was pretty interesting, and I thought that would have caught Putin’s attention and helped him understand that the United States was not going to let go of Ukraine, and that we were going to push back and continue to support them. I think that could have potentially been a turning point. Sadly, that did not come to pass. The White House decided not to send the Tomahawks to Ukraine. But in that moment, it was short-lived, I thought that was a pretty clever way to try and shift Putin’s thinking on the war. But a call from Putin apparently shifted the White House’s position.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIs there anything else you’d be doing at this point if you were in government, whether on the kinds of missiles or other weapons we’re sending to Ukraine or on the diplomatic front? I imagine your approach, if you were carrying out the diplomacy, would be a little different than Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, but there is, I think you hear from a lot of Biden people, regret over not being quite as forward-leaning on some of the diplomacy as you might have been.JULIANNE SMITHYeah. I think the diplomatic efforts would be far more effective if you put people on the job that had decades of experience working with Russia. You are always at risk of getting played by President Putin, given decades of experience in the KGB. And I would recommend that they put some firepower on this and bring in personalities from past administrations. The president seems to have a very positive relationship with Condoleezza Rice, for example. That would be someone who would know full-well what she was up against and how to handle the Russians in those negotiations. H.R. McMaster, someone who had served as a national security advisor in Trump one. Those types of individuals, if you put them on the job, I’d have a lot more confidence. Not to say there would be an automatic breakthrough, but I would have far more confidence than I’ve had in the current team that has tried to negotiate.Of course, the balance has been off. Eight interactions, engagements with Russia, one visit to Ukraine. You can’t possibly move towards some political settlement with that kind of imbalance. That just doesn’t hold. And then I’d love to see the United States return to the leadership role that it had with the Ukraine Defense Contact Group. This is a group that meets monthly. It used to be about 50 countries around the world that was providing weapon systems to Ukraine. It was once led by former Secretary of Defense, Lloyd Austin. And now the United States essentially isn’t leading it, and as I understand it, doesn’t even always join the meetings. I think that matters at the end of the day. Pressure from the United States on other countries to continue providing additional assistance is important. We’d have to return to our old policy of providing security assistance.But I think those types of steps could change the outcome and put us in a much better position where we could work towards some political settlement sooner rather than later.DAN KURTZ-PHELANOne of Zelensky’s pitches, especially to Europeans, but also to some extent to the United States, to Middle Eastern governments, as you noted, to East Asian governments, is that Ukraine will emerge from this war, whenever that is, as the country, at least in the country that is a partner of the U.S. and U.S. allies, that has the most experience with warfare in this age, especially the scale of warfare. And that Ukraine will be a security provider to Europe especially. We saw some of this, as you said, in the Ukrainian assistance to Middle Eastern governments, when they were facing Iranian drones and missile strikes. What would it mean to have Ukraine as a kind of integral part of European defense especially? What does that really mean when Zelensky’s making that pitch?JULIANNE SMITHWell, I think it’s legitimate for him to make that pitch, and I think it’s one where you see a lot of heads nodding across the NATO alliance. Certainly every country on the Eastern flank, most of them would say, “You’re absolutely right, you will emerge from this war as best in class in terms of integrating emerging technology into modern warfare. No one will be able to come close in what you’ve experienced and what you’ve created.” It doesn’t mean that every ally in the alliance needs to mirror that approach and will necessarily fight wars in the same way in the future, but we will have to draw from Ukraine’s experience and learn from them how they have been able to push back on Russian aggression and how they’ve been able in many cases to out-innovate them.And so for NATO, the question is, do you want a country like Ukraine to be outside of the alliance, kind of blowing in the wind, perhaps offering this expertise to anyone who comes knocking? Or do you want Ukraine to be part of the alliance as a strong partner that’s on a path to proper membership, that will bring one of the largest militaries in Europe into the fold with modern technology and know-how that honestly you can’t find anywhere else? I hope the alliance in the future will determine that it is in NATO’s interest to bring Ukraine into the alliance. But as you well know, this is a question that is not yet settled in the alliance, with lots of different views about the risks of doing so. We’ll see what it looks like when the smoke clears in Ukraine. But I think NATO would be mistaken to miss the opportunity to integrate Ukraine into the alliance.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI’m struck that you still see that as not just feasible, but a real possibility and something that a future U.S. administration could and should be advocating.JULIANNE SMITHI hope so. I mean, we had deep arguments over this, as I think has been well documented in the Biden administration, with differences in our own administration and differences across Washington, with congress and with various analysts on the outside. And then deep disagreements across the NATO alliance, with a whole variety of views on the pros and cons of even moving Ukraine slightly closer to the alliance. So it is a hot button issue that’s not yet resolved. We’ll have to see how future U.S. administrations look at it. But my personal view is that this would be additive to the alliance. Of course, we’ll have to see the terms under which the war in Ukraine ends to understand what type of risk the alliance would be assuming if it were to do this.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd you imagine that Russia will do everything it can to try to take this off the table permanently in any kind of settlement?JULIANNE SMITHAbsolutely. I mean, NATO, before the war even started, Russia was trying to get NATO to end enlargement. We had an interesting session in the alliance in mid-January in 2022. We actually had something called a NATO-Russia Council. This was a forum that we created in the 1990s so that NATO could engage in dialogue with the Russians. And so we used that channel in, I think it was January 12th of 2022. And the Russians came into the alliance and essentially demanded that NATO end its history of enlargement, full stop. Not just to Ukraine, but just all of enlargement. And the message that came back was a resounding no, enlargement is actually part of the NATO treaty. In Article 10, it states that the alliance can continue to enlarge. And the allies were not interested in engaging in a conversation about that. We did, however, put forward loads of other ideas trying to encourage them to take an off-ramp and not go to war in Ukraine, but obviously we know how that ended.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThere’s been, as you obviously know and probably hear all the time from your European colleagues, a huge amount of anxiety about the state of the transatlantic alliance and the future of it through the last year-and-a-half or more than a year-and-a-half at this point of the second Trump administration. I’ve detected in, again, much less intensive conversations in the last month or two, a degree of newfound European assurance about the ability of both Europe to survive these changes and the transatlantic alliance to get through it. In contrast to, say, early this year, when the threats over Greenland especially were I think pushing those levels of anxiety to new highs. Do you think that’s right? Do you think there is a level of assurance and that there should be at this point as we look over the next couple of years?JULIANNE SMITHI think it varies depending on where you are, where you’re standing. You might get a slightly different answer in parts of Eastern Europe versus the Nordics versus some of the southern countries of Europe. I do think they feel like they’re on relatively solid ground at the moment. They are happy to hear that there’s been some agreement over Greenland. Many of them say it was a tragedy that it had to erupt into this public dispute over whether or not the U.S. was going to take steps to acquire the sovereign territory of another NATO ally, but they’re on the other side of it. And I think the Danes in particular are hoping that they don’t hear too much about Greenland going forward, and we can just do some good work together in that space.But I think nobody feels like they can rest assured that our behavior will be predictable or that we will be reliable. They still expect twists and turns. The one that they’re quite anxious about right now is the Global Posture Review or the European Posture Review, where the U.S. government, the Pentagon is looking at options right now, and there will likely be some announcement on a possible reduction in U.S. presence in Europe landing sometime around late November, early December. The concern there is that they’re not consulted, that they read about some decision in the paper. There will be something rash, it won’t be gradual, and they’ll be left scrambling to cope with that situation and potentially a crisis, depending on how big the cuts are.So many of them do have a keep calm and carry on attitude of just, “Let’s find a way to find concrete areas to work with the United States and develop deeper cooperation where we can, and deal with the unpredictability in any way possible.” But what I’ve concluded is that there’s a real trust deficit at the end of the day. I mean, trust has always been at the center of our relationship with our closest allies in Europe. And if they don’t trust us, they don’t trust us to show up for some sort of Article 5 contingency or they don’t trust us to share valuable intelligence or bring them into the fold in a moment of crisis, then that fundamentally affects the way that they’re going to interact with us, how much intelligence they may share with us, how frequently they’re going to be willing to follow our lead, how often they’ll believe what we say when we come and warn them about something.So I am worried about the longstanding trust deficit. Could that be rebuilt? Sure, through future administrations. But we shouldn’t be under the assumption that this is a light switch that can be flipped back on. We’ve eroded the trust, and it will take time, many years to reestablish trusting relationships with these close treaty allies.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYour former colleague, Kurt Campbell, wrote in our pages that ultimately the increase in capabilities among both European and Asian allies and the still very strong rationale for these alliances and in some ways growing rationales for these alliances, along with the underpinnings in defense cooperation and technology and everything else, will actually make for a relatively bright future for alliances once you repair those trust deficits.I think what emerged in a conversation—we had a podcast between Kurt and Rush Doshi, another colleague of yours from the Biden administration, and Mark Leonard of the European Council on Foreign Relations on the other side—is that there’s some difference here between the Asian and European allies. But I think certainly Kurt and Rush would argue that there’s at least potential for alliance to be in even better shape five or seven years from now than they were a few years ago. Do you think that’s—I won’t make you argue with Kurt without him here, but curious how you see that basic possibility.JULIANNE SMITHYeah. I listened to that podcast actually, and I was kind of caught in the middle. I had different views on that. I mean, I don’t want to give anyone the impression that the transatlantic relationship is over and we should be issuing last rites. I mean, it’s not that dire. And Kurt was right to point out we’ve weathered many storms over several decades, and I take that point. But I have been traveling quite a bit across Europe and kind of conducting small straw polls wherever I go. And I have asked the question in multiple locations, “If and when a new administration comes in, how would you like to kind of rebuild and refocus the relationship? Where should we focus our energy and where would you be most receptive to a new administration coming in and extending a hand?” Instead of just saying we’re back, which was kind of the tagline from the Biden administration after Trump won.And some of the answers that come back are a little curious. In one capital, the answer was, “Look, all we need to do is keep de-risking from you. And so if you can help us continue to de-risk from the United States, that would be great.” That took me by surprise. And then in other cases, you get more concrete suggestions. Some capitals say, “Look, I think AI is an area where we need to urgently lock arms and work together, and we’d like to see greater cooperation in that space.” China comes up a lot. And so I guess I’m caught between Kurt’s piece and Mark Leonard’s piece on where they land. I do think there’s work ahead and I think there’s the prospect of developing new sets of relationships with our allies. I don’t think we’re going back to where we were.We do have a paradox at the end of the day with Europe. We’re going to be facing, if and when a new administration comes in, the United States will be facing more capable European allies than we’ve seen in many decades, but a relationship that is perhaps more damaged than I’ve ever seen. And so we’ll have to walk through that and determine what does it mean for U.S. leadership and how we interact with our European allies day-to-day.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIf you’re focusing on the NATO piece of that and you’re imagining your successor in a future administration as ambassador NATO, what’s the right way of rebuilding NATO on those new terms? The Trump administration talks about NATO 3.0. Is there a NATO 4.0 or are there elements of NATO 3.0 that you would retain in that case?JULIANNE SMITHWell, maybe it’s just carrying on with the NATO 3.0 analogy, which is now we have an alliance where there’s going to be a stronger European pillar and they’re going to take responsibility for their own security. But they’re also going to want more influence over NATO decisions. They’re going to be questioning U.S. leadership. We may not be able to come into the alliance and kind of command the way forward the way we have over the last seven-plus decades. A little anecdote, when I came into the alliance, I decided in the first few weeks just to listen to allies. And I did that for a couple of weeks, and a couple of perm reps came up to me and said, “What are you doing? You always speak first. You’re the United States. Hit your microphone. And we expect you to speak first and then we’ll respond.”And I wonder for a future ambassador, when he or she arrives on the scene, will they want to hold back and understand where the alliance is right now and listen, or will that demand be made again, “The U.S. speaks first. Tell us where you stand and then we’ll respond to it”? I don’t know. It’s an open question what that relationship will look like at the end of the next two years.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThe other challenge that I think you’d probably have to throw in there at this point is the risk of major political change in Europe with a Marine Le Pen victory in France, potentially growing AFD power in Germany. The UK looks a little bit less likely to see a Nigel Farage victory, but you could see a major change in the political makeup of Europe. How would that change that scenario and present challenges?JULIANNE SMITHYes. Thank you for raising that because that is one scenario that is not all that unimaginary. I mean, it is a real possibility that we could have a shift here in the United States, possibly a Democrat wins in 2028. But then on the other side of the Atlantic, you are facing a collection of leaders on the far-right that now are mirroring some of the positions that we’ve seen with the current U.S. administration, open questions about the utility of NATO membership. Le Pen in France has already stated that she wants to pull France out of the NATO alliance. And the AFD has had some interesting success most recently in state elections.And so I think we do have to ask ourselves the question: who will be our partners on the other side of the Atlantic? And how would they answer that question that I’m kind of peppering with people that I engage in Europe right now, what do you want to build the future relationship on? On which foundation? And the answer may surprise us in some capitals, depending on how their elections go over the next year or two.DAN KURTZ-PHELANOne thing that you pushed hard for when you were ambassador to NATO and which you and Lindsey Ford wrote about in our pages, I believe last year or earlier this year, is about the growing coordination between U.S. allies in Europe and Asia. And why, in the face of growing coordination between U.S. adversaries in Europe and Asia, that cooperation was important or essential. It’s been surprising the Trump administration has been pushing back against that and trying to urge NATO countries to focus on Europe and not spend any time or resources on risk in the Indo-Pacific. What is driving that change and what are the consequences to your mind?JULIANNE SMITHWell, it seems that their theory is that Europe is best suited to focus on its own neighborhood right now, which means two things. One, invest in your own defense and just dig deeper, and make sure you can provide for your own security. And two, make sure you can pick up the slack because the U.S. is cutting off security assistance to Ukraine. So Europe has been kind of assigned to focus on its region. And some of the efforts that we put in place to integrate, for example, the Indo-Pacific partners for countries in the Indo-Pacific into NATO summits and ministerials, those have slipped away. I mean, we did see a few Indo-Pacific countries join the last NATO summit, but certainly it wasn’t given the prominent role that we had assigned it during the Biden administration.So their theory is everybody back to their corners. And I think the good news here is that the genie’s out of the bottle, just to mix metaphors, and that some of the cooperation that we saw that existed across regions, cooperation between Europe and the Indo-Pacific is well underway. Canada is now in the game. Canada is extending a hand to the European Union, moving very closely to deepen that relationship in ways I really wouldn’t have imagined. But even some of the relationships between, say, Japan and the United Kingdom and Italy, where they’re talking about building a sixth-generation fighter without the United States, I mean, these efforts are ongoing. And so I’m not sure that the Trump administration’s efforts to push folks back into their own neighborhoods will ultimately be successful.In fact, I think there’s a risk that the United States wakes up in a few years and realizes that a new web of international cross-regional relationships have started to evolve. And surprise, surprise, the United States is actually not only missing from those relationships, but the United States isn’t leading them. And so it’ll be an interesting moment if and when the new administration comes in ’29 and knocks on the door and says, “Okay, we see what you’ve got going here. Can we have a seat at the table?” And what will the response be? I mean, I suspect hopefully that we’ll be welcomed into some of these mini lateral forums of sorts or different sets of relationships that have moved on without us. But maybe the answer that comes back in some cases is, “We’re good. This is a hedge against you, the United States, and for that reason, we’ll just carry on here over in this side corner.” It will be interesting.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou wrote a piece in Foreign Affairs in 2018 on changing European views of China and the challenges that European governments faced in trying to navigate the growing US-Chinese rivalry that they were caught in the middle of. Seems like, if anything, a tougher position for them now, where they face economic attacks or economic pressure from both the U.S. and from China, as Chinese exports and the effects of that on European industry continue to be a really major preoccupation for them. Do you sense a change in European debates on China? How is that issue shifting in European policy circles, just given the change to much more challenging circumstances now?JULIANNE SMITHSo huge shift, huge shift here in how Europe is looking at China. And this just breaks my heart because we had really reached a point in the Biden administration where it felt like we were starting to speak the same language. That the United States and Europe collectively understood some of the risks of working with the Chinese. We understood some of the tools they were using. The way in which China was deepening its partnership with Russia, and how that created added vulnerabilities for all of us. And the need to join forces to tackle this evolving relationship between not only China and Russia, but frankly with North Korea and Iran as well.Fast-forward to today, I mean, the Europeans are in a difficult position. On the one hand, some of them now want to continue to push forward and take somewhat of a more aggressive stance vis-a-vis China for what it’s doing to Europe’s economies. I mean, I’m thinking about Germany in particular that’s really feeling the weight right now of how China is investing in Europe, ways in which they’re just feeling the weight of their bilateral relationship with the Chinese in real time.But these countries are also facing a difficult relationship with the United States, where they’re motivated to hedge a little bit. And so depending on the capital you’re talking about, I mean, in Spain’s case, we’ve seen Spain move ever closer to the Chinese. Some ways we’ve seen the Canadians do the same thing, to be honest. Germany and France are trying to fight it out right now. Trying to see if they can come together with a united position on this, but they feel a little bit stuck between maintaining a firm line on China for their own security and their own national interests, and then hedging a bit based on the tariffs that the United States still trying to impose in Europe and this topsy-turvy economic and trade relationship that’s unfolding with Washington.So this is, in real time, kind of a test bed for how these capitals are going to handle this dilemma, and I don’t think there’s going to be a united view on this. Like I said, we’re already seeing a number of capitals moving and inching in different directions. The capitals to watch in my mind, though, are really Paris and Berlin, and seeing if those two capitals can come up with some sort of joint position. And that will bring strength to the European Union and then obviously not just to those countries, but other countries that want to join them.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou’ve talked a lot about the challenges that future U.S. administrations will face as they contend with changes in the alliance and changes in the security landscape in Europe and beyond. I’m going to close by just turning the focus back closer to home. You spent a lot of time in the Biden years and before thinking about the domestic political basis for American alliances. I think it’s fair to say that there’s been a shift in certainly democratic voters’ views of traditional American foreign policy. I think it’s probably to some extent more broadly, certainly President Trump taps into this. How do you see that as a constraint driver of future foreign policy options, and what’s the right way of responding to that if you’re thinking about future administrations?JULIANNE SMITHWell, you’re right, we don’t know what type of candidate we’re going to have on the Democratic side of things, and there are now splits across the party on a variety of issues. Not huge gaps, but some differences. And we do have some folks that, I mean, really on the right and the left, that continue to see value in pushing the Europeans to take on a greater burden and to step back from some of the responsibilities that we traditionally have held around the world, not just in Europe, but in the Indo-Pacific and the Middle East and elsewhere. And so first and foremost, we have to see what kind of candidates are we going to be looking at on the right and the left, and how are they going to talk to the American people about alliances and our relationships with our closest partners and allies around the world?And they’re going to have to do that by testing and engaging in real conversations. Where I think Americans generally land is that they do understand the tagline “stronger together,” and that while Europeans may not be as capable as the United States, they do bring capacity. If you’re looking for capacity, there’s no better place to look than Europe. And Europeans still are additive in whatever we’re tackling, artificial intelligence, a military operation, a cyberattack. You want to do it with partners and allies.And so I don’t think it’s so hard to get Americans to have some buy-in on, look, Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea have assembled their team on the field. Who’s on our team? Who’s on team America, on the other end of the field? I think that’s not hard to talk about. But I guess the hardest part of it will be getting down to the details. Do you want the United States to continue to be the leader in all of these institutions? How much more reform will be needed? Can we afford to make these commitments and have presence all around the world when we’re facing so many challenges on the home front? We’ll have some fierce debates about the defense budget, for example.So all of this will be part of the, I think, conversation across the country, and I don’t think it’s limited to one party or the other. I mean, I think you can find different views among Republicans and among Democrats, and so it’ll be a live debate, but one that’s frankly probably overdue. And so I think it’s important to, I don’t know, test where Americans are right now and see how they want to assemble that team on the field, and what type of kit they want to provide to that team, what kind of investment do they want to make in those types of relationships overseas?DAN KURTZ-PHELANI suspect the European piece of that conversation will be much less fraught than the discussion about the Middle East, but still will be a complicated one.JULIANNE SMITHFor sure. For sure.DAN KURTZ-PHELANBut, Julie, thanks for the great recent piece and pieces you’ve done since leaving government, and thanks so much for being back on the podcast.JULIANNE SMITHThanks. It’s great to be back.
